assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics gave a unified formal and empirical account of how electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal institutions shape policy outcomes. It created a field and reaches well beyond economics into comparative politics. It sits close to the institutions and growth agenda recognised in 2024 but is distinct from it.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the core pair, with the joint books and papers on constitutions and electoral rules. Besley's work on state capacity and accountability is a substantial parallel strand. A three-person prize is defensible, though Besley's share is the least clear-cut.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly three decades, has been replicated and extended widely, and is part of standard graduate training. There is no timing risk.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer Persson and Tabellini alone.
Possible perceived overlap with recent institutions-related prizes.
Causal identification in the cross-country constitutional work is weaker than in the best micro-empirical literatures.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks are a foundational mechanism in macro-finance. They underpin modern analysis of credit cycles, financial crises and macroprudential policy. The 2008 crisis and its aftermath confirmed the relevance of the mechanism.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is the clear originating contribution and is cleanly attributable to the two of them. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the financial accelerator strand, which overlaps with the 2022 prize and should not dilute the core pair.
assessment.maturity: It has nearly three decades of citation, extension and policy use. It is mature and was strongly validated empirically after 2008.
uncertainties: Committee appetite for another macro-finance prize after 2022.
Overlap with the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator literature.
The original model is stylised, and the empirical identification of the mechanism is mostly done by others.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm model of trade reoriented the field. It moved analysis from industries and countries to firms, and it brought selection effects and new gains-from-trade channels into both theory and empirical work. It is influential for policy and measurement.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central paper. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple extended it to exporting versus FDI, and Helpman's wider contributions to new trade theory are well documented. Redding is a plausible third name but with a smaller claim on the core discovery.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of extensions and heavy empirical use. It is clearly mature.
uncertainties: Whether Helpman is better credited here or with Grossman (B004).
Whether the Krugman prize (2008) makes the committee cautious about another trade-theory award.
Credit for firm-level empirical precursors, such as Bernard and Jensen, is outside the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Task-based accounts of technological change and the measurement of trade-shock effects reshaped understanding of labour demand, wage inequality and the local consequences of globalisation. The work has major policy and public-debate impact and uses transparent empirical designs.
assessment.attribution: The skill-biased change and polarisation strand (Autor, Katz and collaborators) and the China-shock strand (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) overlap only partly. Katz's contribution is distinct from the China-shock work, so a three-person grouping is somewhat composite. Dorn is a real co-author of the China-shock papers and could be argued for instead.
assessment.maturity: Roughly three decades for the education-technology race and polarisation work, and about a decade for the China shock. The core findings have mostly held up, though some magnitudes are debated.
uncertainties: Fit between the two strands.
Size of the China-shock effects and robustness of the shift-share instruments.
Proximity to the Acemoglu technology and inequality agenda and to Goldin's 2023 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This line combines sufficient-statistics reasoning with the empirical elasticity of taxable income, so optimal-tax theory can be applied to administrative data. It has changed how tax policy is analysed and evaluated, and is among the most consequential recent work in public economics.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod and Feldstein-era work on taxable income elasticity precedes Saez, and Feldstein is deceased. Chetty's contributions are split across this line and mobility work (B038). Stantcheva's work is newer. Credit is therefore spread, and the three-name limit forces some omissions.
assessment.maturity: The core elasticity and sufficient-statistics work is two decades old and well replicated. Parts of the optimal-taxation framework are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap of Saez and Chetty with other ballot entries (B038, B050).
Debate over elasticity estimates and behavioural responses.
Selection of three from four or more strong names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Demand estimation with differentiated products (BLP) and dynamic industry models gave industrial organisation a common empirical toolkit. It is widely used in merger review, antitrust and regulatory analysis, so it has substantial practical impact beyond academia.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes are the identifiable BLP trio, with Pakes also central to dynamic-game estimation (Ericson-Pakes, Olley-Pakes). Bresnahan and others have an earlier claim on parts of the structural IO agenda, but the three-name limit makes the BLP trio the cleanest choice.
assessment.maturity: BLP is from 1995 and has been in continuous use ever since. It is highly mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a method more than a discovery.
Competing claims from Bresnahan, Reiss and others in structural IO.
Identification and computational concerns in BLP-style estimation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, the Calvo pricing model, the Taylor rule and the microfounded New Keynesian synthesis form the basis of central-bank modelling and the practice of monetary policy. The influence on policy is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit is widely dispersed among Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum, Smets and others, and a three-person limit makes any selection contestable. Taylor (rule and staggered contracts), Calvo (pricing) and Woodford (synthesis) are the most separable foundational contributions.
assessment.maturity: More than three decades of use, the framework has been stress-tested, and parts have been revised after 2008.
uncertainties: Many equally deserving names are excluded.
The framework is partly collective and incremental.
Policy and political controversy around the Taylor rule, and whether the 2022 monetary prize reduces appetite.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The intertemporal approach to the open economy, including the 'Redux' model and the exchange-rate disconnect puzzles, shaped modern international macroeconomics. It is a pervasive framework and a textbook organising principle for analysis and policy.
assessment.attribution: Obstfeld and Rogoff are the clear pair, with their joint 1995-96 papers and textbook. Other contributors to open-economy macro, such as Sachs, Svensson and Lane, are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of use. The empirical puzzles they identified remain only partly resolved.
uncertainties: Rogoff also appears on B007, so some attribution overlap exists across ballot entries.
Whether the contribution is seen as a framework rather than a discovery.
Competition from other macro entries in the same cycle.
